meta.audience: His children and his brethren, and readers of the plates

world_behind.title: Metal versus everything else
world_behind.text: Verses 1 and 2 give the reason for engraving: what is written on plates remains, and what is written on anything else perishes. Papyrus and parchment were the ordinary media of the period and both rot. The chapter's opening argument is a materials argument, and it is the plainest statement in the record of why anyone would go to this trouble.

world_behind.title: A stated audience of descendants
world_behind.text: The writing is addressed to "our children, and also our beloved brethren," and the hope is that they will read without contempt "concerning their first parents." Ancient records are usually addressed to a king, a god, or posterity in the abstract. This one names the risk that posterity will be embarrassed by it.

world_behind.title: The Isaac binding read as similitude
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says Abraham's obedience was accounted to him for righteousness and that the offering of Isaac was a similitude of God and his Only Begotten. Jewish and Christian readers had both worked that comparison; what is distinctive here is that it is offered as the reason a colony keeps the law of Moses at all.

world_behind.title: "Looking beyond the mark."
world_behind.text: The phrase occurs nowhere else in scripture. A mark is a target, and archery is the natural picture: the arrow overshoots because the eye was fixed past the thing aimed at. Jacob makes it a diagnosis of scholarly failure, and that is why the sentence stings.

world_behind.title: The rejected stone, before the rejection
world_behind.text: Verses 15 through 17 read Psalm 118's head of the corner and Isaiah's sure foundation as prophecy about a stumbling that has not yet happened. The gospels apply the same two passages after the fact. Here they are used to predict, and the prediction is dated roughly five hundred years early by the record's own reckoning.

world_behind.title: A prophet naming his own limit
world_behind.text: Verse 18 makes the whole of the next chapter conditional on Jacob not getting shaken from his firmness. Ancient prophetic books do not usually pause to say the author might lose his nerve. The sentence is the last thing before the longest allegory in the record.

words.text: A likeness that instructs. It is the King James word for a figure that teaches by resemblance rather than by identity. Jacob applies it to an event, so the binding of Isaac becomes a piece of enacted teaching. The word carries the whole weight of why the law is kept in this colony.

The word describes what has been shaken and did not move. Jacob names what produced it before he names it: the prophets searched, the revelations, the spirit of prophecy, and "having all these witnesses we obtain a hope" (v. 6). Only after that list does the faith arrive, and with it the claim about trees and mountains and waves. The last verse of the chapter puts the same root back in play, this time about himself. The King James Bible does not use the word; in this record it belongs to faith that has been through something, as when Enos says his became unshaken after his long struggle in prayer (Enos 1:11).

cites.quote: having all these witnesses we obtain a hope

spans.text: having all these witnesses we obtain a hope

words.text: Plural here, and singular everywhere else it appears. Treated at 2 Nephi 9:53. The angel asked Nephi whether he knew the condescension of God, and the answer given there was the incarnation. Jacob uses the plural for the ordinary, repeated coming-down that lets weak people do anything at all, which extends a term that had named one event.

Not merely unknown but not findable by searching. Paul uses it of God's judgments (Rom. 11:33) and the wisdom books use it of kings' hearts (Prov. 25:3). Placed next to "it is impossible that man should find out all his ways," it concedes the limit before the chapter tells anyone to stop despising revelation, and that order matters.

To give counsel. The word appears once in this record and never in the King James Bible. Jacob uses it to close a two-way sentence: do not counsel the Lord, take counsel from his hand, since he counsels in wisdom, in justice, and in great mercy. The same verb runs both directions, and only one direction is open.

Under the law the firstfruits are the first sheaf of a harvest, carried to the priest before anyone eats from the field (Lev. 23:10). The sheaf stands for a crop still in the ground. Paul gives the term to Christ, risen and "become the firstfruits of them that slept" (1 Cor. 15:20), and Lehi had used it of him in the same way (2 Ne. 2:9). Jacob puts his hearers in that position instead, "presented as the first-fruits of Christ unto God" (v. 11), so the people are what gets carried in, and the harvest they stand for is his.

cites.quote: presented as the first-fruits of Christ unto God

spans.text: presented as the first-fruits of Christ unto God

phrases.term: Whatsoever things we write upon anything save it be upon plates must perish
phrases.text: A sentence about decay, written by a man engraving metal. Nothing in it is metaphorical. It states why the labor is worth it, and it turns the physical awkwardness the previous chapters complained about into the reason the reader has anything at all.

phrases.term: That they may learn with joy and not with sorrow, neither with contempt
phrases.text: Three possible receptions, listed in descending order, and two of them are bad. Jacob is imagining a descendant reading this and being ashamed. He does not defend against it; he names it and keeps engraving, which is the most human sentence in the chapter.

phrases.term: We knew of Christ, and we had a hope of his glory many hundred years before his coming
phrases.text: The record's own account of what it is for: a demonstration that this knowledge was held early and by others. Everything the chapter goes on to argue about the law of Moses and the prophets is in service of this one claim about timing.

phrases.term: For this intent we keep the law of Moses, it pointing our souls to him
phrases.text: A stated reason for observance, which the record rarely supplies. The law is kept and it is subordinated in the same clause. The verb is directional. The law points, and what it points at is a person.

phrases.term: The very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea
phrases.text: An extraordinary claim, made in passing, in a subordinate clause, on the way to something else. Jacob does not illustrate it or offer an instance. The next verse immediately reassigns the power to grace, and the sequence is the point: the claim is made and then given away.

phrases.term: The Lord God showeth us our weakness that we may know that it is by his grace
phrases.text: Weakness is presented as something shown instead of something suffered. The showing is deliberate and instructional, and its purpose is attribution. This is the record's tightest statement of why capable people are kept aware of what they cannot do.

phrases.term: Seek not to counsel the Lord, but to take counsel from his hand
phrases.text: The pun is in the verb. To counsel is to advise; to take counsel is to receive advice, the same word running both directions in a single line. The correction being offered is a specific reversal of who is advising whom.

phrases.term: Why not speak of the atonement of Christ
phrases.text: An argument from consistency, put as a question. If a resurrection and a world to come can be known and discussed, there is no reason the atonement should be off limits. Jacob is answering an objection the text never states, which suggests he had heard it.

phrases.term: Of things as they really are, and of things as they really will be
phrases.text: The record's definition of what the Spirit does, and it is about knowing rather than about feeling. Two tenses, one adverb, no qualifier. It has become the standard scriptural formula for truth in this tradition, and it stands in a chapter about why plain speech matters.

phrases.term: Their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark
phrases.text: A mark is a target set up to be shot at, and the whole sentence hangs on that: the blindness comes from aiming past the target. Cause is supplied for a condition the prophets normally just assert, and the cause is over-reaching that looks like seriousness. What follows is worse. God gave them what they wanted, which was things they could not understand, so that they would stumble.

phrases.term: The stone upon which they might build and have safe foundation
phrases.text: Two Old Testament stone passages folded together and applied to an event centuries out: Isaiah's tried and precious corner stone and the psalm's rejected head of the corner. Jacob treats the stone as already identified, names no name, and moves on to the question of whether a rejected foundation can be rebuilt on.

phrases.term: If I do not, by any means, get shaken from my firmness in the Spirit
phrases.text: The chapter's last clause is a condition on the next chapter. Jacob attributes the risk to "my over anxiety for you," which makes the threat to his composure a pastoral one. He is worried about caring too much to think straight.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: Why anyone engraves
verses.text: Difficulty of the medium, permanence of the medium, and then the hope attached to it: that descendants will read with joy rather than with sorrow or contempt. Three verses that are entirely about the act of writing, placed at the head of the chapter that will explain what the writing is for.

verses.label: v. 4–6
verses.title: The purpose, and the credentials
verses.text: The record states the purpose of its own writing in a purpose clause, and it is about a future reader's knowledge of a past writer: "for this intent have we written these things, that they may know that we knew of Christ." Verse 5 then supplies a reading of Genesis 22 that the source does not contain, calling Abraham's offering of Isaac "a similitude of God and his Only Begotten Son." Verse 6 lists what searching the prophets produced, in an order that escalates from revelations and the spirit of prophecy to hope, unshaken faith, and command over "the very trees" and "the mountains, or the waves of the sea." Six items, ending in a claim that can be tested by whether the record ever reports such a thing being done.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: The correction, immediately
verses.text: Weakness is shown so that power is credited to grace; the depths are unsearchable; no one knows God's ways unless they are revealed; therefore do not despise revelation. Then the argument from creation. If speech made the world and the man, commanding the earth is a smaller thing. The chapter's boldest claim is defended by its least controversial one.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: Counsel, reconciliation, and permission to speak
verses.text: Do not advise God; be reconciled through the atonement; obtain resurrection and be presented as first-fruits; and then the question, why should the atonement be harder to speak of than the resurrection? Three verses that move from posture to doctrine to method.

verses.label: v. 13–14
verses.title: Plainness, and what happens without it
verses.text: Prophesy to the understanding of men, because the Spirit speaks things as they are and will be. Then the counter-example: a people who despised plainness, killed the prophets, sought what they could not understand, and were given exactly that. The two halves are a rule and its violation, in that order.

verses.label: v. 15–17
verses.title: Led into prophecy
verses.text: Jacob says he is being led by the Spirit into prophecy, and the prophecy is that the stumbling produces a rejection, that the rejected stone is nevertheless the only sure foundation, and that the question of how a people rebuild on something they threw away is left open. He asks it and does not answer it.

verses.label: v. 18
verses.title: A promise, hedged
verses.text: The record makes a promise and attaches a condition that could void it, in one sentence: "I will unfold this mystery unto you; if I do not, by any means, get shaken from my firmness in the Spirit, and stumble because of my over anxiety for you." The risk named is not opposition or ignorance but the speaker's own concern for the audience. Jacob 7:26 supplies the same writer's summary of that condition years later, "we did mourn out our days," and 2 Nephi 32:7 records another writer stopped mid-sentence, "the Spirit stoppeth mine utterance." Here the interruption is anticipated rather than reported, and the allegory of Jacob 5 follows because it did not occur.

chapter.title: The chapter is the record explaining itself
chapter.text: Verses 1 through 4 state the medium, the audience, and the purpose of the entire project: to show later readers that this knowledge of Christ was held early. Nothing else in the record makes that case so directly, and everything after verse 4 is evidence for it.

chapter.title: Power is claimed and reassigned within two verses
chapter.text: Trees, mountains, and waves obey in verse 6; verse 7 says God shows them their weakness so the credit lands on grace. The order is unlikely to be accidental, and it recurs in this record whenever spiritual capacity is described. Jacob does not qualify the claim; he relocates its source.

chapter.title: "Looking beyond the mark" names a failure available only to serious people
chapter.text: The people described are not careless. They searched, and they searched past what was there. That is why the diagnosis has traveled so far beyond its original target, and why the chapter pairs it with an instruction to prophesy to the understanding of men.

chapter.title: God is described as granting a request that ruins the requester
chapter.text: Verse 14 says they desired things they could not understand, and that God gave them what they desired so that they would stumble. The record states this without softening. It is one of the hardest sentences in the book, and it sits between two verses about plainness.

chapter.title: The stone question is left open on purpose
chapter.text: Verse 17 asks how a people who rejected the foundation can build on it and does not answer. The allegory in the next chapter is the answer, and Jacob flags it as a mystery he will unfold. The chapter is structured as a setup, which is why it ends mid-thought.

chapter.title: The writer's nerve is presented as a variable
chapter.text: Verse 18 makes the delivery of the next chapter contingent on Jacob's own steadiness, and attributes the risk to excessive concern for his audience. A record this careful about authority is unusually frank about the state of the man holding the pen.

chapter.title: Plainness is argued for on grounds of what the Spirit is like
chapter.text: Verse 13 does not say plain speech is kind or effective. It says the Spirit tells the truth about things as they really are, so prophecy should be intelligible. The style is derived from the source.

applications.title: Write it on something that lasts
applications.text: Jacob's argument is about media. Take one thing you want your descendants to know and put it somewhere durable and findable, in a format that will still be readable in twenty years.

applications.title: Assume a reader who might be embarrassed by you
applications.text: Write anyway, and write in a way that gives them something to learn from. Jacob names contempt as a possible reception and keeps going.

applications.title: Say why you keep what you keep
applications.text: Pick one practice you maintain (a habit, an observance, a rule) and articulate what it points at. If you cannot, that is information.

applications.title: Relocate the credit before you need to
applications.text: When something goes well because of your capacity, say out loud where the capacity came from. The chapter builds the reassignment into the same paragraph as the claim.

applications.title: Stop counseling God
applications.text: Notice how much of your praying is advice. Try one prayer that is entirely receiving counsel rather than giving it.

applications.title: Aim at the mark
applications.text: Identify one area where you have made a simple thing complicated in the name of depth, and go back to what was actually being asked.

applications.title: Prophesy to the understanding
applications.text: When you teach or explain, strip it to what your hearer can actually use. Jacob grounds plainness in the nature of the Spirit.

questions.text: What am I leaving behind, and would the people who find it learn from it or wince at it?
What do I do religiously that I could not explain the purpose of if asked tomorrow?
When was I last shown my weakness, and did I read it as failure or as instruction?
In what part of my life am I advising God rather than asking him?
What true thing do I avoid speaking about because it feels presumptuous?
Where am I looking past the mark, making a plain requirement complicated because the complication is more interesting?
What have I not said because I care too much about how it will land?
